The color of your FTS Maroon Monster plants is interesting. Mine rarely show much green; instead, they're slathered in red:



This is eastern North Carolina, with an average amount of sunshine (dawn until 2 PM). I took this picture in early September, so this coloration wasn't motivated by cold temperatures. My plants were like this all summer long.

posts.body_html:
maroon monster here also usually is solid red, but that pot was grown shaded by some sarracenias, so it only got afternoon sun.

Here's a "new" selection from the Onslow Co, NC population that I call Dark red. This will be an absolute interesting breeder clone, I haven't made any crosses with it yet, but plan to do so! Pics taken 10/24/22:





A lot of flytraps can get this deep red. Even typicals can if you grow them under greenhouse conditions. What's special about this clone is that it gets dark red outdoors while other clones in the exact same conditions don't get quite so red! I bet this clone can produce traps as dark as maroon monster if greenhouse grow! Notice the plants in the foreground, they are also from ONslow Co, NC and grown in the exact same soil, repotted at the exact same time, and grown under the exact same microclimate, but aren't as red:

posts.body_html:
venus fly traps exposed to multiple hard freezes versus light frost! It's mostly cosmetic, I've notice no difference in health the next grow season. Pics taken mostly December 2022:


Here are the plants exposed to the elements, 100% perfect health and fully dormant. They've been growing outside all season long, so they're strong and can take the cold. These got hit with temperatures below 25F multiple times (down to 21F so far), and probably 40 nights so far with frost:


And these were exposed only to light frost (no lower than 29F). These are placed by the house. Why? Well, the cephalotus (background) can't take hard freezes. Some of the flytraps just acclimated to outdoor conditions right before going dormant, so they're potentially frost sensitive for the first dormancy period. After that, once they've been grown outside all season long, the large plants can take it!

posts.body_html:
Here are some older photos of Dionaea RG38N. For those of you who thought that stands for Dionaea REAL GANGSTER at 38North Latitude, you are probably not right. For the rest of you (probably 100% of people reading this), you didn't think it meant that....RG actually stands for Ron Gagliardo, who is/was famous for being one of the main growers at the Atlanta Botanical Gardens!

This photo was taken a few years ago, but it just goes to show that this clone is consistently a winner year after year! For those of you who grow flytraps, you'll know not many clones consistently perform well all the time....this one does, at least outdoors here in Northern California!


Spilling out of the pot here, ladies and gentlemen (and the rare gangster who also likes carnivorous plants), photo taken 10/13/23:

updated post on some new clones to the collection:


BCP H-15, love this one:


The famous Dionaea Wine Mouth, hasn't yet colored up like in the photos but it's still very new to the collection:


GJ Phalanx, famous for those long teeth! I almost lost this clone due to neglect, but it was repotted last winter and has taken off! This clone is quite vigorous and relatively easy to grow:


Dionaea Ghost, a variegated clone. This clone is reportedly one of the more easy to color up ones, many of the other clones rarely if ever get variegated despite having the genes for it. It has colored up here outdoors in Northern California, no artificial suntan or greenhouse/LED lights:


Dionaea Bimbo, an absolute winner! Traps get really dark, moreso than many other non-all red clones. This is also reportedly able to produce large traps, but the clone is still new to the collection, so I haven't gotten it to it's fullest size potential just yet:


Another shot:


UK Sawtooth: vigorous, easy to grow, and good looking!


To be continued.....

posts.body_html:
I'm very impressed with Dionaea Chinese Dumpling, it's vigorous, colorful and relatively easy to grow. You can't say that about many of the mutant flytraps: most of those are super finicky, super slow, and just don't perform well until years of babying them! These photos are literally a few months after I acquired this plant, which has been TC'ed:









Same clone about a month earlier, this was prior to placing it in full sun. It was completely green/light starved when I first got it and very fragile, took a lot of babying to get to this stage:


And here's BCP Z11, a new favorite. This is during the dormancy period, I totally forgot to photograph it a few months ago! It looks way better when in full growth:



Here's BCP
